title: Hosted API - Chat & Generation Basics: streaming, params, retries
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a hosted API demo for QuillForge focusing on chat generation basics: streaming, parameter tuning, and retry strategies. Customer is evaluating hosted option for chat features (low-latency reqs) and asked about cost/latency tradeoffs, SOC2/data residency, and how retries/backoff work in the client and server. SE showed live console, streaming example, and Optimize suggestions for batching/caching. Agreed next steps: send pricing, security pack, and a short PoC checklist + test account.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-09
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Ruiz (QuillForge CTO), Mark Benson (Lead Eng), Priya Shah (Product), Tom (intern)

Summary / Agenda (auto-generated): Quick intros, high-level hosted API capabilities, live demo (chat streaming + params), retry/backoff strategies, console observability, Q&A, next steps.

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this account, with Ravi our solutions engineer. Quick round robin?
[00:00:12] Elena Ruiz: Hi Maya, Elena here, CTO at QuillForge. We're looking at adding a chat assistant into our product, low latency but cost sensitive.
[00:00:21] Mark Benson: Mark, lead eng, we'll likely run initial pilot on hosted, then evaluate dedicated if throughput grows.
[00:00:28] Priya Shah: Priya from product, focused on UX and safety filters.
[00:00:32] Ravi Patel: Great, thanks. I'll do a short demo. Note: recording may be a little noisy, apologies for any transcription typos — like our "Redwood Dedicate" sometimes shows up in transcripts.

[00:01:05] Ravi Patel: Ok, starting with a simple hosted API chat example. I'll show two flows: non-streamed single response, and streamed token-by-token so the UI can render progressively. First, curl example for a simple generation: POST /v1/chat/completions, body with model, messages, temperature, top_p, max_tokens.
[00:01:33] Mark Benson: Quick question — do you support stop sequences for multi-turn conversation?
[00:01:38] Ravi Patel: Yep, stop tokens are supported. You can pass an array. Also we have "structured output" helpers if you want JSON-in-response enforcement. Note that sometimes the transcriber flips "topP" to "top pea" in the automated transcript, so ignore that.

[00:02:05] Ravi Patel: Now streaming: we stream as chunked HTTP / SSE — each event contains partial tokens and partial deltas. Benefits: perceived latency is much lower for users. Drawbacks: more connections, need client-side concat logic, and if you have caching we can cache prefixes but not in-flight tokens.
[00:02:35] Elena Ruiz: For our mobile app, we prefer streaming. How does retrying work with streaming? If a connection drops mid-stream, does Redwood replay?
[00:02:45] Ravi Patel: Good question. The server doesn't automatically re-stream the same session mid-response. Best practice: use an idempotency key per user message + a small buffering window. Our recommended pattern: attempt a network-level retry on transient errors, but if you got partial stream, you should reconcile client-side and if needed re-issue request with the same idempotency token so the server returns the same full response. That avoids double writes to logs and keeps semantics stable.
[00:03:20] Maya Chen: I'll also note we have short-lived session tokens and request IDs in logs — helpful for debugging replay cases.

[00:04:00] Ravi Patel: Let's talk params — temperature controls randomness, 0.0 deterministic-ish, 0.7 creative. top_p is nucleus sampling; they interact. max_tokens caps the output; presence_penalty/ frequency_penalty apply for repetition control. We recommend starting with temperature 0.2-0.4 for assistants that should be consistent.
[00:04:32] Mark Benson: Any guardrails for hallucination?
[00:04:35] Ravi Patel: Two parts: model choice & prompt engineering, plus post-processing checks. On Redwood Optimize we can monitor quality regressions using eval sets and flag drift. Also the console supports per-route safety filters (regex/email blockers, etc.).

[00:05:10] Ravi Patel: Retry strategies — we suggest exponential backoff with jitter. For idempotent operations (like generation when you provide an idempotency token) you can safely retry. For streaming specifically, there's a nuance: if your client times out before receiving final token, re-issuing with same idempotency token tends to return the cached final result if available. If not cached, it's a new run.
[00:05:42] Elena Ruiz: So caching is prefix-aware? Can you cache at the tokenizer level?
[00:05:48] Ravi Patel: We do KV cache and prefix caching; we can cache cached prefix completions depending on your model and quantization choices. It's part of the Optimize suggestions: if 70% of requests share first 40 tokens, Enable prefix cache reduces cost notably.

[00:06:30] Priya Shah: Can you show the console now?
[00:06:33] Ravi Patel: Yep. (screen share) Console overview: per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdown, latency P50/P95/P99, request traces, and a streaming gauge for active connections. You can also set per-route throttles and a fallback policy to switch to a smaller model if latency spikes.
[00:07:10] Maya Chen: Quick note on models: hosted catalog includes curated open models and Redwood-verified performance profiles. We also provide recommended quantization and kernel settings for each model.

[00:07:40] Mark Benson: How are rate limits applied? Per-key? Per-project?
[00:07:44] Ravi Patel: Rate limits can be per-API key and per-route. For enterprise we can map to project/team and have dedicated pools. If you need guaranteed throughput, Redwood Dedicated is the path; but for many customers hosted with tuned batching and prefix cache is enough.

[00:08:10] Elena Ruiz: Security questions — SOC 2, encryption at rest, KMS?
[00:08:15] Maya Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II, customer-managed KMS options for Private deployments, and encryption at rest for hosted. I'll attach the security pack after the call.

[00:09:00] Ravi Patel: Back to streaming error modes: client disconnected, server OOM, transient network. Each has different observability signals in console. For OOMs we typically route to a smaller model automatically (graceful degradation) so you don't see an outage.

[00:09:30] Mark Benson: Do you recommend using smaller models as fallback or returning short canned reply?
[00:09:35] Ravi Patel: Both are supported. Fallback policy config has options: model_fallback -> smaller model, region_fallback, and canned_response. It depends on product experience — for UX you'd want the assistant to degrade gracefully but maintain clarity.

[00:10:00] Priya Shah: Can we see a live streaming sample?
[00:10:03] Ravi Patel: Sure, I'll run a sample from the SDK in Node. (typing sounds) Example: client.chat.stream({model: 'rf-2-small', messages, temperature:0.25}) then on 'data' events push to UI.
[00:10:20] Ravi Patel: (demo) You can see tokens arrive with partial deltas and role changes. Note: sometimes separators or punctuation are delayed depending on decode step.

[00:11:05] Tom: quick — can we cancel in the middle of a stream?
[00:11:08] Ravi Patel: Yes, you can. Client-side cancel will send a termination to the runtime; runtime will stop compute and free the KV cache. If you later re-request with same idempotency token, you might get a cached final if it was already completed and cached.

[00:11:35] Elena Ruiz: How do you bill streaming vs non-streaming? Token-based still?
[00:11:39] Maya Chen: Billing is token-based for both. We bill on tokens generated; streaming just affects how tokens are delivered, not metering. We show a token breakdown per-route in Console.

[00:12:10] Mark Benson: Any built-in retry headers or client libs that handle backoff?
[00:12:15] Ravi Patel: Our SDKs include default retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter. They also surface hooks to customize. For high-QPS customers we recommend tuning concurrency and configuring retry budgets to avoid thundering herds.

[00:12:45] Ravi Patel: Let's cover concurrency — per-request CPU/GPU saturation metrics are in the console. For high-concurrency, we propose a combination of: 1) batching (where latency SLO allows), 2) lighter model families for quick replies, 3) dedicated pools if you need guaranteed compute.

[00:13:18] Priya Shah: Could you explain batching without increasing latency for users?
[00:13:22] Ravi Patel: Continuous batching groups in-flight requests within a short micro-window (tens of ms) so you gain throughput with minimal added latency. If you need strict single-digit ms latency, batching may be limited. Optimize will suggest batching tide based on observed inter-arrival times.

[00:14:05] Ravi Patel: I'll show an Optimize view. (screen share) Optimize flags: batching.score, prefix_cache.hit_rate, quantization_recommendation. For example, it suggested 4-bit quantization for rf-2-medium for your throughput profile which drops GPU memory and allows higher concurrent contexts.

[00:15:00] Mark Benson: Anything about evaluation monitoring? We want regression alerts when model changes reduce accuracy on critical prompts.

[00:15:05] Ravi Patel: We offer eval suites where you can push a set of prompts and baselines. Console has regression alerts on any delta beyond thresholds. You can gate rollouts by eval pass/fail as part of canary deploys.

[00:15:40] Elena Ruiz: Latency SLOs — P95 target?
[00:15:44] Maya Chen: For hosted, typical P95 is 200-600ms for small models under normal load, P99 longer. We publish benchmarks per-model; we can share a performance spreadsheet. If you need 100ms P95 we usually recommend Dedicated or careful model selection + edge routing.

[00:16:10] Mark Benson: On the topic of retries, are there idempotency token size limits?
[00:16:14] Ravi Patel: Keep tokens short — UUID or hashed composite key. We recommend a 36-char UUID or similar. The server stores mapping for a retention window (configurable).

[00:16:40] Ravi Patel: Now a quick example of a retry with idempotency token in the SDK. (demo) If the request returns 5xx, our SDK will do up to 4 retries with backoff; for non-idempotent semantics you can disable retries.

[00:17:10] Priya Shah: For GDPR/data residency, can logs be restricted?
[00:17:13] Maya Chen: We support data residency options and redaction rules. For hosted customers, logs are encrypted and can be scoped to region. For strict regulatory requirements we have Private (VPC/on-prem) with customer-managed control plane.

[00:18:05] Mark Benson: Let's talk about quotas — we may spike occasionally. Do you support burst capacity?
[00:18:10] Ravi Patel: Hosted supports burst up to an envelope; Dedicated has configurable burst policies. We can also provision burst credits for pilots.

[00:19:00] (demo continues) Ravi shows a request trace where a single user message is traced through prefix cache hit -> model infer -> stream out. The UI shows token-meter, cost estimate, and trace id.

[00:19:38] Ravi Patel: Note: trace ids are handy if you need Redwood to debug an anomaly — include the trace id and time range when you open a support ticket.

[00:20:05] Elena Ruiz: Any limits on concurrent streaming connections per key?
[00:20:09] Ravi Patel: There's a soft limit; it depends on plan. We throttle by default to protect fair usage. For enterprise plans we can raise the limit.

[00:20:50] Priya Shah: Regarding safety, are there prebuilt content filters?
[00:20:54] Ravi Patel: Yes, console has safety rules; plus you can plug in post-processing hooks to call internal or third-party moderation. We also provide a safety scoring output sometimes labeled in logs.

[00:21:30] Mark Benson: Pricing model question — token units vs reserved capacity?
[00:21:34] Maya Chen: Hosted is token-based pricing with tiered rates; Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commit. For pilots token is easiest; as you scale we can model TCO and propose Dedicated or a hybrid.

[00:22:05] Elena Ruiz: Do you have a sandbox account we can use for stress tests?
[00:22:09] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll provision a test project with limited credits. That will let you validate streaming behavior and retries under load.

[00:22:40] Ravi Patel: A couple of gotchas we've seen: 1) mixing different idempotency semantics in client libs leads to duplicate responses. 2) Large max_tokens + high concurrency can push memory usage — watch P95 cost and tune quantization.

[00:23:20] Priya Shah: If we do a PoC, what's the recommended measurement window?
[00:23:24] Ravi Patel: 2 weeks typically — enough to capture variability. Collect logs for P50/P95/P99, prefix cache hit rates, and failure modes. Optimize can ingest telemetry to generate recommendations.

[00:24:00] Mark Benson: Can you send an example benchmark sheet?
[00:24:03] Maya Chen: Will attach the perf spreadsheet along with pricing and a short PoC checklist.

[00:24:30] Tom: (inaudible) question about SSE vs websockets?
[00:24:33] Ravi Patel: Both are supported; SSE is simpler for mobile/HTTP clients, websockets give more bidirectional control. Choose based on your app stack.

[00:25:10] (brief pause, background typing)

[00:25:40] Elena Ruiz: Any notes on model updates — will model version changes happen without notice?
[00:25:45] Maya Chen: We try to avoid silent regressions. For hosted models we publish change logs and you can pin model versions. We also provide rollout controls so you can opt-in to new model variants.

[00:26:10] Ravi Patel: Example: canary rollout — 5% traffic to new model for 24 hours, monitor eval metrics, then ramp. Console can automate the rollouts.

[00:26:50] Priya Shah: On safety filters, can we add domain-specific blocklists?

[00:26:54] Ravi Patel: Yes, you can upload blocklists or use regex rules per route. We also allow transform hooks to pre-process prompts.

[00:27:30] Maya Chen: We're approaching mid call — any particular deep dives you want after this? Dedicated ops, deeper cost modeling, or security?
[00:27:36] Elena Ruiz: Let's do a follow-up technical PoC kickoff for infra — bandwidth, expected qps, and storage.

[00:28:00] Ravi Patel: Cool. Back to streaming: in terms of implementation patterns, some customers use a hybrid approach: stream partial tokens for UX, then at completion call a non-streaming request for a canonical final reply for logging and analytics. That simplifies downstream processing.

[00:28:35] Mark Benson: That seems useful. Any downsides?
[00:28:38] Ravi Patel: Double-run cost if you don't use idempotency/caching. But if you pass same idempotency token and server has cached final, cost is minimal.

[00:29:05] Priya Shah: Show me the SDK snippet again for JS and python?
[00:29:08] Ravi Patel: (reads snippets) JS: client.chat.stream(...).on('data', d=>...). Python uses iterator yield. We'll email both snippets.

[00:30:00] (demo shows a trace for a failed stream to illustrate retry)

[00:30:22] Ravi Patel: In this example the edge returned 503; SDK retried with backoff, and because idempotency token matched, the second attempt returned same final.

[00:30:50] Elena Ruiz: Any SLA on retries?
[00:30:53] Maya Chen: Retries are client-configured; SLA is about uptime and latency targets. We do have an enterprise SLA for Dedicated. For hosted there's a published availability target.

[00:31:20] Mark Benson: Can we integrate with our SSO for Console access?

[00:31:23] Maya Chen: Yes, SAML/SSO and RBAC supported. We'll add your admin user after contract stage.

[00:31:50] (short silence as people scroll)

[00:32:10] Ravi Patel: One more Optimize tip: if you have many short requests, using higher batching window might actually increase end-to-end latency but reduce cost, so Optimize will tell you the sweet spot.

[00:32:45] Priya Shah: For the PoC checklist, can you include logging fields we should capture?

[00:32:50] Maya Chen: Yes — request_id, trace_id, model_version, prompt_hash, idempotency_key, latency_ms, token_count. We'll include that in the checklist.

[00:33:20] Mark Benson: Ok, let's talk timelines — if we spin a PoC next week, what support do we get?

[00:33:25] Maya Chen: We'll assign a solutions engineer and provide onboarding docs, plus a short runbook. Ravi can be primary SE.

[00:33:50] Elena Ruiz: Cost sensitivity — is there volume discount?

[00:33:54] Maya Chen: Yes, we have tiered pricing and pilot discounts. We'll model it after we see expected qps and token mix.

[00:34:20] Ravi Patel: Quick demo wrap: streams, params, retries, backoff, idempotency tokens, console observability.

[00:34:35] Priya Shah: Will you share a short diagram of recommended client architecture (stream + final canonical)?

[00:34:39] Maya Chen: Yep, we'll include that in the follow-up email.

[00:35:10] (Questions from Tom about websocket reconnection handling — Ravi answers)

[00:36:00] Ravi Patel: A couple of troubleshooting tips: 1) correlate trace ids, 2) use SDK logs at debug level to inspect partial deltas, 3) if you see high P99 latencies check prefix_cache hit-rate.

[00:36:45] Elena Ruiz: Anything we should watch for in post-launch?

[00:36:49] Ravi Patel: Monitor hallucination metrics, prefix_cache hit-rate, token per request, and error rate. Set alerts on P95 latency and error budget.

[00:37:20] Mark Benson: Are there hooks for us to export logs to our SIEM?

[00:37:24] Maya Chen: Yes, log export to S3, BigQuery, or streaming to your SIEM is supported. We'll include the integration docs.

[00:37:50] (brief discussion about contract terms, not detailed)

[00:38:20] Ravi Patel: Wrapping up — recommended next steps: provision sandbox, run 2-week PoC, collect telemetry, run Optimize recommendations, then evaluate Dedicated if necessary.

[00:38:40] Maya Chen: I'll send an email with pricing, SOC2, sample snippets, the PoC checklist, and the perf spreadsheet.

[00:39:05] Elena Ruiz: Sounds good — can we schedule the technical kickoff for next Wed?

[00:39:10] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll propose times.

[00:39:30] (closing pleasantries)

[00:39:45] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. Ravi — anything to add?
[00:39:48] Ravi Patel: No, just ping me with your qps.

[00:40:00] (call ends; people say thanks)

Notes about transcript quality: automated transcript has occasional mis-attributed speakers and some product names mis-spelled (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate").
